what: Cemig is the electricity utility of Minas Gerais, a large state in Brazil. It generates power, mostly from hydroelectric dams, operates the distribution network delivering electricity to millions of customers in the state, and also distributes natural gas.
customers: Households, businesses and industry in Minas Gerais receiving electricity through its regulated distribution network, plus wholesale electricity and gas customers.
money: Regulated electricity delivery to customers across Minas Gerais.
Hydroelectric and other generation, sold under contract and into the market.
Natural gas distribution through its Gasmig subsidiary.
moat: Electricity distribution in a defined territory is a legal monopoly with tariffs set by the Brazilian regulator, which makes the revenue predictable and the position permanent. Its hydroelectric plants are long-lived assets on sites that cannot be replicated. Minas Gerais is one of Brazil’s largest and most industrialised states.
risks: The state government is the controlling shareholder, which means political considerations can influence decisions that a purely commercial owner would make differently.
Brazilian regulated tariffs are set by the government, and tariff reviews have squeezed distributors before.
Hydroelectric output depends on rainfall, and drought forces expensive market purchases to meet contracts.
Revenue swung from $7.6B in 2023 to $6.4B in 2024, reflecting energy costs and currency rather than the business.
Only three analysts cover the stock, so the $2.22 average target rests on very thin coverage.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 5.5 times earnings and 0.68 times sales — very low multiples for a regulated utility.
Trailing net income of $937.6M on $7.5B of revenue, with free cash flow of $509.8M.
A monopoly distribution franchise in a large industrial state produces predictable, inflation-adjusted revenue.
Hydroelectric generation has almost no fuel cost and very long asset lives.
Brazilian utilities have historically paid large dividends, and the regulated cash flow supports them.
watch: Hydroelectric generation volumes and regulated tariff review outcomes. Rainfall sets the cost of serving customers and the regulator sets what can be charged.
view: Cemig is a regulated monopoly utility in a large industrial Brazilian state, trading at 5.5 times earnings. The business is about as predictable as businesses get — people in Minas Gerais need electricity, nobody else may sell it to them, and the regulator allows a return on the invested network. The discount is entirely about Brazil and about who controls the company.

The ownership point deserves to be stated plainly because it is the central issue. The state government is the controlling shareholder. That means decisions about tariffs, dividends, investment and employment can be influenced by political considerations that a purely commercial owner would weigh differently. This is not hypothetical in Brazil — state-controlled utilities have been directed toward outcomes that served the government rather than minority shareholders. Any investor here is a minority partner to a politician.

The operating variables are rainfall and the regulator. Cemig’s generation is substantially hydroelectric, which is wonderful when it rains — almost no fuel cost, century-long asset lives — and expensive when it does not, because the company must buy power on the market to meet its contracts. Brazil has had extended droughts, and that is the single largest source of earnings surprise in this business.

The revenue line is not worth following: it swung from $7.6 billion to $6.4 billion and back, which reflects energy costs passing through and currency translation rather than anything about the company. At 5.5 times earnings with $510 million of free cash flow, this is cheap, and Brazilian utilities have historically paid large dividends from exactly this kind of regulated cash flow. The honest assessment is that it is cheap for reasons — political control and currency — that are unlikely to disappear, so the return has to come from the dividend rather than from a re-rating.
bull: A monopoly franchise in a large industrial state keeps generating regulated cash flow, hydro costs stay low, and 5.5 times earnings funds a large dividend.
bear: The state government directs the company toward political rather than commercial outcomes, drought forces expensive power purchases, and the real weakens against the dollar.
